children: on Wednesday said its Raytheon Australia business has completed the delivery and preparation of a new air defense system for the Australian Army, marking the end of a multiyear development and integration project.

The National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System, commonly known as NASAMS, is now considered combat-ready. That means the equipment has been delivered, connected and tested, while Australian soldiers have been trained to operate it.
The system is designed to detect, follow and potentially shoot down aircraft, drones and cruise missiles before they reach troops, military bases or other important infrastructure.

NASAMS links several components into a single defensive network. Radars search the sky and identify possible threats. A command center processes that information and helps operators decide which target to engage. Mobile launchers then fire missiles selected for the type and range of the threat.

Australia’s version includes locally designed radars from CEA Technologies. It also uses a Fire Distribution Centre from Norway’s Kongsberg, which serves as the system’s command-and-control hub by combining radar information and coordinating launch decisions.

Raytheon’s mobile missile launcher is mounted on the Australian-built Hawkei protected vehicle. This allows Army units to move the system between locations rather than relying on permanent launch sites.

The package can fire several Raytheon missiles, including the standard AMRAAM, the longer-range AMRAAM-ER and the AIM-9X. The missiles were originally developed for aerial combat but can also be launched from the ground against airborne targets.

A multispectral ground system provides additional surveillance using different kinds of sensors. In plain terms, it can help operators identify threats using more than one part of the light spectrum rather than depending exclusively on conventional radar.

The combat-ready declaration is primarily an execution milestone for RTX rather than a new contract award. It demonstrates that Raytheon can integrate NASAMS with locally produced equipment and military vehicles, potentially strengthening the system’s appeal to other countries seeking customized air defenses. Rising demand for protection against drones and cruise missiles also supports the longer-term market for NASAMS, missile replenishment and maintenance. However, RTX disclosed no new order value, revenue forecast or additional Australian procurement tied to the announcement.
Demand extends beyond the initial delivery
Raytheon Australia said it adapted the baseline NASAMS design for Australian conditions and operational requirements. The company also trained Australian soldiers to use the system.

NASAMS is described as a short-range air defense system, meaning it protects a limited geographic area rather than intercepting ballistic missiles or other threats hundreds of miles away. Its modular design lets military customers combine different radars, command systems, launchers and missiles.

RTX said combat use of NASAMS has contributed to international demand and that it is investing to increase production. The company did not specify how much additional manufacturing capacity it plans to add or when that capacity will become available.
